items.stem: On a tree diagram, to find the probability of a combined outcome along a path you should
options: add the probabilities along the branches
subtract the probabilities
multiply the probabilities along the branches
divide the probabilities
items.answer: multiply the probabilities along the branches

items.stem: Explain why the probabilities on the second branches change when counters are taken without replacement.
items.answer: After the first counter is removed there are fewer counters in total and possibly fewer of that colour, so the probabilities for the second pick depend on the first.
items.markingKey: B1 total decreases; B1 depends on first outcome (dependent) [2]

items.stem: Explain why P(at least one six in two throws of a die) is found by 1 − P(no sixes).
items.answer: "At least one six" includes several paths; the only other outcome is "no sixes", so it is quicker to subtract P(no sixes) = 25/36 from 1, giving 11/36.
items.markingKey: B1 complement covers all other outcomes; B1 11/36 [2]

multiply the probabilities of the paths
subtract the smaller from the larger
add the probabilities of the paths

items.stem: The probabilities on the branches from one point of a tree diagram

add up to 0

items.answer: It can happen as red then blue or blue then red; these are mutually exclusive, so their probabilities are added.

items.stem: What does A ∩ B mean?
options: The number of elements in A
The elements in A or B or both
The elements in both A and B
The elements not in A
items.answer: The elements in both A and B
items.markingKey: Intersection: in A and in B.

items.stem: Explain why n(A ∪ B) is not always equal to n(A) + n(B).
items.answer: Elements in both A and B would be counted twice, so n(A ∩ B) must be subtracted: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

items.stem: Explain what it means for two sets to be disjoint and how this appears on a Venn diagram.
items.answer: They have no elements in common (A ∩ B = ∅); the circles do not overlap.

items.stem: Explain the difference between P(A | B) and P(A ∩ B).
items.answer: P(A ∩ B) is the probability that both happen, out of all outcomes; P(A | B) is the probability of A among only the outcomes where B happens.
items.markingKey: B1 both out of all; B1 restricted to B [2]

items.stem: Explain why P(A | B) is usually not equal to P(B | A).
items.answer: They use different restricted groups: P(A | B) divides by P(B), P(B | A) divides by P(A); these are only equal if P(A) = P(B).

items.stem: A survey gives locals: museum 28, beach 23, market 27; tourists: museum 10, beach 17, market 18. Mateo wants the probability that a person chose museum, given that they are one of the tourists, and writes 10/123. Explain the error and give the correct probability.
items.answer: "Given that" restricts the choice to the 45 tourists, so the probability is 10/45 = 2/9.

items.stem: The table shows the results of a survey: Year 10 students: walking 20, bus 13, car 17; Year 11 students: walking 16, bus 8, car 6. A person who chose car is selected at random. Find the probability that they are in Year 10 students.
Of 40 families in a street, 16 own a cat, 13 own a dog and 3 do both. A person is chosen at random from those who own a cat. Find the probability that they also own a dog.
A bag contains 5 red and 6 blue counters. Two are taken at random without replacement. Given that both are the same colour, find the probability that both are red.
items.markingKey: M1 P(both red) = 2/11; M1 P(same) = 5/11; M1 divide; A1 2/5.

items.stem: A screening test for a disease is used in Bangkok. 1/25 of the people tested have the disease. If a person has the disease, the probability of a positive test is 9/10. If a person does not have the disease, the probability of a positive test is 3/50. (a) Given that a person tests positive, calculate the probability that they have the disease. (b) Comment on how likely it is that a person who tests positive actually has the disease. (c) In a group of 1000 people, estimate how many would test positive.
items.answer: (a) 5/13 ≈ 0.385 (b) Most positive results are false positives, because the disease is rare; a second test would be needed. (c) 93.6
